evidence.text: At 20 workers: 20 useful jobs/second and 1 second mean service time.
At 40 workers: 13.3 useful jobs/second and 3 seconds mean service time.
Database wait time rises; worker CPU remains below saturation.

observations.statement: At 20 workers: 20 useful jobs/second and 1 second mean service time.
At 40 workers: 13.3 useful jobs/second and 3 seconds mean service time.
Database wait time rises; worker CPU remains below saturation.

hypotheses: Shared database contention may extend service time.
Retries or a changing document mix may also affect useful throughput.

experiment.action: Hold the document mix fixed and reduce concurrency in small steps.
experiment.rollback_condition: Abort if oldest pending job age exceeds the predefined SLA threshold.

uncertainty: No query-level trace or fixed-workload comparison is available.
baseline.exercise: Choose an initial action. Which two measurements would distinguish contention from retry amplification? What result would reverse your decision?

evidence.text: Attempt rate rises after an external processing service begins timing out.
Unique completed jobs fall while redelivered messages increase.
The current retry loop immediately resubmits failed requests.

observations.statement: Attempt rate rises after an external processing service begins timing out.
Unique completed jobs fall while redelivered messages increase.
The current retry loop immediately resubmits failed requests.

hypotheses: Immediate retries may amplify dependency overload.
A subset of permanently invalid inputs may be consuming attempts.

experiment.action: Separate transient failures from invalid input; test bounded delayed retries with jitter.
experiment.rollback_condition: Pause the experiment if unique completion rate falls or the oldest pending job breaches its time budget.

uncertainty: The failure distribution and downstream capacity limit are unknown.
baseline.exercise: Explain why an increasing attempt rate can coexist with declining throughput. What must be idempotent before retrying?

evidence.text: An analytical dashboard responds in 200 ms in this fixture.
A recently updated assessment does not appear for 15 minutes.
The operational database already contains the update.

observations.statement: An analytical dashboard responds in 200 ms in this fixture.
A recently updated assessment does not appear for 15 minutes.
The operational database already contains the update.

hypotheses: Processing lag may violate the product freshness requirement.
A cached response or mismatched filters may conceal a fresh record.

experiment.action: Compare source timestamps, processing watermarks, and cache state for the same assessment.
experiment.rollback_condition: Do not accept a latency improvement that breaches the agreed freshness budget.

uncertainty: The acceptable freshness target and cache configuration are unspecified.
baseline.exercise: Which requirement is missing? How would you distinguish processing lag from a stale cache before changing databases?
